reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Machine Learning & External Data
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 14, the final module of IAN 601. This module is intentionally designed as a bridge into the machine learning course you will take next semester.

We are not going to begin with a complicated algorithm. We will begin with something familiar: a simple algebraic formula.

From there, we will ask what happens when the formula is unknown and we only have examples.

[tts-break]

That idea leads naturally into machine learning.

We will move from a known line, to learning the line from data, to noisy observations, residuals, multiple features, numeric vectors, regression, classification, train and test data, evaluation metrics, and prediction.

The purpose is to make machine learning feel like a continuation of what you already know rather than a completely separate subject.

By the end, you should understand the structure of an ML workflow even if you have not yet studied every algorithm.

slides.title: Why end IAN 601 with machine learning?
slides.transcript:
Machine learning brings together many ideas from this course.

Python gives us the programming foundation. NumPy and Pandas give us arrays, Data frames, vectors, and numerical representations. Data cleaning helps us improve input quality. Statistics and visualization help us understand distributions and relationships before modeling.

[tts-break]

Machine learning adds a new goal: learning a relationship from examples so we can make predictions for new cases.

That means the work you have already done is not separate from machine learning. It is the foundation.

Next semester, you will learn more algorithms and more advanced evaluation techniques. But those methods will be much easier to understand if you already know what features are, how data becomes numeric, why we separate training from testing, and why model evaluation must use unseen data.

slides.title: What does a model actually do?
slides.transcript:
At its simplest, a model is a rule that maps an input to an output.

If we already know the rule, we can write it directly.

For example, if y equals two x plus one, the model is already known. Give me x, and I can calculate y.

Machine learning becomes useful when the exact rule is unknown or too complicated to specify manually.

[tts-break]

Instead of writing every coefficient ourselves, we provide examples and let an algorithm estimate the relationship.

That is why I want you to think of machine learning as learning a useful mathematical rule from data.

The output of the learning process is still a model.

The model takes features as input and produces a prediction.

This basic structure appears again and again, whether the algorithm is linear regression, logistic regression, a decision tree, a neural network, or something much more complex.

slides.title: Start with algebra: y = 2x + 1
slides.transcript:
We begin with a relationship that we already know: y equals two x plus one.

Here, two is the slope and one is the intercept.

If x is one, y is three. If x is two, y is five. If x is three, y is seven.

Because the relationship is linear, these points fall on a straight line.

[tts-break]

Run the Python code and look at both the x and y values and the plot.

Then change the slope from two to three and run it again. Notice how the line becomes steeper.

Change the intercept from one to five and observe how the line moves upward.

This is not machine learning yet because we already know the rule.

But it gives us the mathematical structure that a linear model will later try to learn from data.

slides.title: Reverse engineer the formula from data
slides.transcript:
Now we make the problem more interesting.

Suppose the equation is hidden. We only observe the points one comma three, two comma five, three comma seven, four comma nine, and five comma eleven.

We can see that they appear to follow a straight-line pattern, but we pretend we do not know the formula.

[tts-break]

The Linear Regression model receives the x values and the known y values and estimates the slope and intercept.

Run the code and inspect the learned coefficients.

You should see a slope very close to two and an intercept very close to one.

This is our first machine learning example.

The algorithm is reverse engineering the relationship from examples.

The model learns parameters from data instead of receiving the formula directly from us.

slides.title: Real data is noisy
slides.transcript:
Perfect lines are useful for learning, but real data is rarely perfect.

Measurements contain noise. People behave differently. Important variables may be missing from the dataset. Sensors can contain error. Real processes have natural variation.

So even when an underlying linear relationship exists, the observations usually do not sit exactly on one line.

[tts-break]

Run the example and look at the scattered points.

The Linear Regression model still finds a best-fit line through the data.

Notice that the line does not pass through every point.

That is expected.

The purpose of the model is not necessarily to memorize every training observation. It is to capture a useful overall relationship that can generalize to new data.

This difference between fitting patterns and memorizing data becomes very important later in machine learning.

slides.title: What does “best fit” mean?
slides.transcript:
If the fitted line does not pass through every point, how does the algorithm decide which line is best?

For each observation, the model makes a prediction.

The difference between the actual value and the predicted value is called a residual.

If the actual value is ten and the prediction is nine point two, the residual is zero point eight.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the residuals.

The dashed vertical segments in the plot show the distance between each observed point and the fitted line.

Machine learning algorithms often choose model parameters by minimizing some measure of overall error, called a loss function.

You do not need to master optimization in this course.

The important idea is that training means adjusting model parameters so predictions fit the training examples according to a defined objective.

slides.title: From one x to many features
slides.transcript:
So far, we have used one input variable, x.

Real prediction problems usually use several inputs.

Imagine predicting an order amount using customer visits, pages viewed, previous orders, and days since the last visit.

Instead of one x, we now have x one, x two, x three, and x four.

[tts-break]

The algebraic structure is still familiar.

A multiple linear model combines an intercept with a coefficient multiplied by each feature.

The model learns those coefficients from the training data.

This is an important connection: machine learning with many features is still built on the idea of inputs being combined mathematically to produce an output.

The number of features can become very large, but the conceptual structure remains the same.

slides.title: Features become numeric vectors
slides.transcript:
Machine learning algorithms usually expect numerical input.

One observation can be represented as a vector.

For example, a customer might be represented as seven visits, sixteen pages viewed, two previous orders, and fifteen days since the last activity.

That becomes a numeric vector with four positions.

[tts-break]

When we place many observations together, the vectors form a matrix called X.

Rows represent observations. Columns represent features.

This is one reason NumPy and Pandas were important earlier in the course.

A Data frame is convenient for people because it includes column names and labels. Underneath, many machine learning algorithms operate on numerical arrays and matrices.

When you see capital X in machine learning code, think feature matrix.

slides.title: What if a feature is text?
slides.transcript:
Not every useful feature begins as a number.

Suppose the sales channel is Web, Store, or Email.

A linear model cannot multiply a coefficient by the word Web.

So we need to create a numeric representation.

One common method is one-hot encoding.

[tts-break]

Run the example and see how Pandas creates separate indicator columns.

If the observation belongs to Web, the Web column becomes one and the other channel columns become zero.

The feature is still categorical in meaning, but the model now receives numbers.

This idea is called representation.

Different types of data require different representations.

In your next machine learning course, you will see preprocessing tools that perform these transformations automatically inside pipelines.

slides.title: Regression versus classification
slides.transcript:
Supervised machine learning often begins with two major problem types: regression and classification.

Regression predicts a numeric value.

Examples include predicting a house price, sales amount, temperature, or hospital length of stay.

Classification predicts a category or class.

Examples include yes or no, fraud or not fraud, or one of several diagnosis categories.

[tts-break]

Both problem types use features, targets, training data, fitted models, and evaluation.

What changes is the type of target, the algorithms we may choose, and the metrics used for evaluation.

In this module, we first used linear regression to connect algebra with learning.

Now we will move into binary classification using logistic regression, where the target has two values: responded or did not respond.

slides.title: Supervised learning workflow
slides.transcript:
The word supervised means that the training examples include the correct target.

During training, the model receives X, the feature matrix, and y, the known target values.

The algorithm uses those labeled examples to estimate model parameters.

After training, the fitted model receives a new feature vector and produces a prediction.

[tts-break]

This sequence is central to supervised learning.

Known examples teach the model. New cases test whether the learned pattern generalizes.

You will see this same pattern with many algorithms next semester.

The internal mathematics may be different, but the workflow remains recognizable: collect labeled examples, represent them numerically, fit the model, evaluate on unseen data, and then use the model for new predictions.

slides.title: External data sources
slides.transcript:
Real machine learning projects rarely begin with a small Data frame typed directly into Python.

Data may come from CSV or TSV files, Excel workbooks, APIs that return JSON, or databases queried with SQL.

The technical loading step is only part of the problem.

[tts-break]

You also need to understand data provenance.

Who produced the data? What does each field mean? When was the data collected? How often is it updated? Are you allowed to use it for this purpose?

Those questions are especially important in machine learning because a model can learn patterns that reflect the limitations or biases of the source data.

External data must still go through the same quality and interpretation checks you learned earlier in the course.

slides.title: Read external CSV data
slides.transcript:
CSV is one of the most common formats for tabular data.

In the browser example, the CSV is stored as text so the code can run without downloading a separate file.

In VS Code or Jupyter, you would normally pass a file path to read CSV.

[tts-break]

After loading the data, do not jump directly into modeling.

Inspect the Data frame. Check the shape, column names, data types, missing values, and target values.

Machine learning workflows often fail because the analyst assumes the input is ready without checking it.

Loading data is only the first step.

A good modeling workflow treats inspection and validation as part of the pipeline, not as optional preparation.

slides.title: JSON and API-style data
slides.transcript:
APIs often return JSON rather than a simple table.

JSON can contain nested structures, such as a customer object containing an activity object with visits and order counts.

Pandas provides tools such as json normalize to flatten those nested records into columns.

[tts-break]

Run the example and inspect the resulting table.

In a real API project, you also need to read the API documentation, understand authentication, respect rate limits, and handle errors.

Never publish a private API key in a notebook or GitHub repository.

External data access is both a technical and security responsibility.

The goal is to transform the external response into a stable, well-defined feature table that can be inspected and analyzed.

slides.title: Inspect modeling data before fitting
slides.transcript:
Before fitting a model, inspect the modeling dataset carefully.

Check for missing values, strange ranges, duplicates, inconsistent types, and class imbalance.

Also ask whether each feature would actually be available at the moment the prediction is needed.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the target counts.

If the classes are highly imbalanced, accuracy may become misleading.

For example, if ninety-five percent of cases are class zero, a model that predicts zero every time already achieves ninety-five percent accuracy.

Data quality remains important because machine learning does not automatically know which values are mistakes.

A model can learn an incorrect pattern just as efficiently as a correct one.

Good modeling starts with good data inspection.

slides.title: Correlation matrix: inspect numeric relationships
slides.transcript:
A correlation matrix gives us a quick view of pairwise linear relationships among numeric variables.

The values range from minus one to plus one.

The plot uses a matrix layout so we can inspect many variable pairs at once.

Run the code and look at both the numbers and the visual pattern.

[tts-break]

Correlation can help us notice features that move together or variables that appear related to the target.

But do not treat high correlation as proof that a feature is important, useful, or causal.

Two features can be highly correlated with each other and still add little new information to a model.

A nonlinear relationship can also be useful even when linear correlation is low.

Use the correlation matrix as an exploratory tool, not an automatic feature-selection rule.

slides.title: Separate features X and target y
slides.transcript:
Machine learning code commonly separates the input features from the target.

X is the feature matrix.

y is the target vector.

In our example, X contains visits, pages viewed, past orders, and days since the last activity. The target is responded.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the shapes.

Each row in X corresponds to one target value in y.

Also look at the first feature vector as a NumPy array. This makes the matrix idea concrete.

It is extremely important that the target does not accidentally appear inside X.

If the answer is included as an input, the model will appear to perform very well for the wrong reason.

That is a simple example of data leakage.

slides.title: Train/test split
slides.transcript:
A model should not be evaluated only on the data it used for learning.

We therefore separate the dataset into training data and test data.

The training set is used to estimate the model parameters.

The test set is held aside and used later to evaluate performance on unseen cases.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the shapes.

The random state makes the split reproducible, which means you and your students can get the same partition each time.

Stratify helps preserve the proportion of the target classes in both training and test sets.

This separation is one of the most important ideas in machine learning.

Training asks, can the model learn from examples?

Testing asks, does what it learned generalize to data it did not see during fitting?

slides.title: Start with a baseline
slides.transcript:
Before celebrating a model's accuracy, compare it with a simple baseline.

For classification, a useful baseline is predicting the most common class every time.

This sounds simplistic, and that is exactly the point.

The real model should add value beyond a trivial rule.

[tts-break]

Run the baseline code and record the accuracy.

Later, compare that number with logistic regression.

If the machine learning model performs about the same as the baseline, it may not be learning anything useful.

Baselines give performance context.

They prevent us from being impressed by a number that only looks good because the prediction problem is easy or the classes are unbalanced.

Always ask, better than what?

slides.title: Logistic regression: from a linear score to probability
slides.transcript:
Logistic regression is a useful bridge between the linear algebra we started with and classification.

First, the model creates a weighted linear score.

That score looks similar to a multiple linear regression equation: intercept plus coefficients multiplied by features.

Then logistic regression passes that score through a sigmoid function.

[tts-break]

The sigmoid converts the score into a value between zero and one, which we interpret as a probability.

That is why logistic regression can be used for binary classification even though the word regression appears in the name.

The linear part combines the features.

The sigmoid turns the result into a probability.

Then a decision threshold can convert that probability into a class label.

slides.title: Visualize the sigmoid curve
slides.transcript:
The sigmoid function is an S-shaped curve.

Its input, z, can be any real number.

Its output always stays between zero and one.

When z equals zero, the probability is one half.

Large positive scores move the probability toward one. Large negative scores move it toward zero.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect the curve.

Notice that the probability changes most rapidly around the center.

The important connection is this: logistic regression still creates a linear score from the features, but instead of treating that score as the final prediction, it transforms the score into a probability.

This visualization helps explain what the model is doing mathematically without requiring advanced calculus.

slides.title: Train a logistic regression classifier
slides.transcript:
Now we put the classification workflow together.

We create X and y, split the data, create a Logistic Regression model, fit it on the training rows, and then predict the test rows.

Run the code and compare predicted labels with the actual labels.

[tts-break]

Remember that the model has not seen the test targets during training.

That is why the comparison is meaningful.

If we only evaluated the model on its training data, we would be measuring how well it fits known examples rather than how well it generalizes.

This train-fit-predict pattern appears across many supervised algorithms.

Next semester, you may replace Logistic Regression with a decision tree, random forest, support vector machine, or another classifier, but the surrounding workflow will look very familiar.

slides.title: Confusion matrix
slides.transcript:
Accuracy gives us one summary number, but it does not tell us which mistakes the model made.

A confusion matrix separates predictions into four categories.

True negatives and true positives are correct predictions.

False positives are cases predicted positive that were actually negative.

False negatives are actual positives that the model missed.

[tts-break]

Run the code and inspect both the numeric matrix and the visual confusion matrix.

Think about the meaning of each error.

In a medical screening problem, a false negative could mean missing a patient who actually has the condition.

In a spam filter, a false positive could mean moving an important legitimate email into spam.

The importance of each error depends on the application.

That is why evaluating classification requires more than accuracy alone.

slides.title: Accuracy, precision, recall, and F1
slides.transcript:
Different classification metrics answer different questions.

Accuracy asks what fraction of all predictions were correct.

Precision asks, among the cases predicted positive, how many were actually positive.

Recall asks, among the actual positive cases, how many did the model find.

F1 combines precision and recall into one measure.

[tts-break]

Run the classification report and compare the metrics.

Do not try to memorize formulas first.

Focus on the questions each metric answers.

In some applications, recall matters more because missing a true positive is costly.

In others, precision matters because false alarms are expensive.

There is no universally best metric.

The correct evaluation depends on the decision the model will support and the consequences of its mistakes.

slides.title: Probability threshold changes the decision
slides.transcript:
A classifier often produces a probability before producing a class label.

The threshold determines when the probability becomes class one.

A common default is zero point five.

If the probability is at least zero point five, predict one. Otherwise, predict zero.

[tts-break]

Run the example and then change the threshold to zero point three.

You should see more positive predictions.

Change it to zero point seven and you should see fewer.

This tradeoff affects false positives, false negatives, precision, and recall.

The default threshold is not automatically the best threshold for every application.

The appropriate choice depends on the costs and goals of the real decision problem.

slides.title: Predict a new case
slides.transcript:
After a model is trained, we can use it on a new observation.

The new customer must have the same feature meanings used during training: visits, pages viewed, past orders, and days since the last activity.

Run the code and inspect both the predicted class and predicted probability.

[tts-break]

Then change one or two feature values and see how the probability responds.

The model is applying the relationship it learned from the training examples.

But remember that a probability is not certainty.

It is the model's estimate based on the training data, selected features, learned parameters, and assumptions.

A prediction should always be interpreted together with the model's evaluation results and limitations.

slides.title: Avoid data leakage
slides.transcript:
Data leakage occurs when the model receives information that would not truly be available when the prediction is needed.

A simple example is including the target itself inside the features.

Another example is using information that is only known after the outcome happened.

Leakage can also happen during preprocessing if information from the test set influences transformations fitted before evaluation.

[tts-break]

Leakage is dangerous because it can make a weak model appear extremely accurate.

Then, when the model is used in the real world, that future or target information is no longer available and performance collapses.

For every feature, ask: would I genuinely know this value at prediction time?

That question is one of the best practical defenses against leakage.

slides.title: Use a pipeline for consistent preprocessing
slides.transcript:
Preprocessing should be applied consistently to training, test, and future data.

A scikit-learn Pipeline allows us to connect transformations and the model into one object.

In the example, the pipeline first standardizes the numeric features and then trains logistic regression.

[tts-break]

The important benefit is not only convenience.

The scaler learns its parameters from the training data.

When test data arrives, the same learned transformation is applied without refitting on the test set.

That helps prevent leakage and keeps the workflow reproducible.

Next semester, you will likely build larger pipelines that include missing-value imputation, categorical encoding, scaling, feature selection, and the model itself.

The same basic pattern begins here.

slides.title: End-to-end machine learning workflow
slides.transcript:
This slide brings the entire workflow together.

Start with a question. Bring in external data. Inspect and clean it. Define features and the target. Split into training and test sets. Fit the model. Evaluate it against a baseline. Then use the fitted model for new predictions.

[tts-break]

The Python example demonstrates the core technical stages using a Pipeline.

But a real machine learning project continues beyond one notebook.

Models need monitoring. Data distributions can change. Performance can drift. New data may require retraining. Privacy, fairness, documentation, and operational constraints also matter.

For now, focus on recognizing the structure.

If you understand this workflow, you already have the conceptual map you need for a much deeper machine learning course.

slides.title: Practice challenge
slides.transcript:
Now build the classification workflow yourself.

Begin by inspecting the data and target balance.

Create X and y, then create a stratified train and test split.

Build a majority-class baseline.

Train logistic regression and compare its performance with the baseline.

[tts-break]

Calculate accuracy and a confusion matrix.

Inspect predicted probabilities and then create one new customer for prediction.

Finally, write two limitations of the model.

Do not write everything at once.

Build the workflow one stage at a time and inspect the output after each step.

The goal is not only to make the code run.

The goal is to understand why every stage exists and what could go wrong if you skip it.

slides.title: IAN 601 course wrap-up
slides.transcript:
You have now reached the end of IAN 601.

Across the course, you moved from Python fundamentals into reusable functions, NumPy arrays, Pandas Data frames, data cleaning, exploratory analysis, statistics, visualization, external data, and introductory machine learning.

Those topics may look different, but they are connected by one analytical workflow.

[tts-break]

We begin with a question.

We represent data in a useful form.

We inspect quality.

We transform and summarize the data.

We select an appropriate method.

Then we interpret the result and communicate its limitations.

The most important habit I want you to carry forward is this: always connect the code to a question, the output to an interpretation, and the interpretation to the limits of the evidence.

That habit matters in every data analytics project.

slides.title: Next semester: Machine Learning & Predictive Analytics
slides.transcript:
Next semester, your machine learning course will go much deeper.

You may study linear and logistic regression in more detail, followed by decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, nearest-neighbor methods, cross-validation, model tuning, feature engineering, class imbalance, clustering, neural networks, and other predictive methods.

[tts-break]

You do not need to memorize all of those algorithms now.

The important foundation is already in place.

You understand that observations become feature vectors, many feature vectors form X, targets form y, training estimates model parameters, test data evaluates generalization, and metrics help us understand performance.

You also understand that leakage, data quality, and interpretation matter as much as calling fit and predict.

That foundation will make the next course easier to follow because the algorithms will fit into a workflow that you already understand.
